question: Tell me about a time you waited for instructions and it cost the work. What did you change after?

raiseTranscript.text: I was building a small dashboard component and waited two days for the exact API contract from the backend owner. The sprint ended without the feature, which pushed a demo. After that I started writing down my assumptions in the ticket and pinging the owner with a proposed contract if I hadn't heard back in 24 hours.
What happened the next time a spec was unclear?
I flagged it in standup the same day and shipped a stub version that the PM could review.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you waited for instructions and it cost the work. What did you change after?
Role: new grad on small UI task
Situation: waited for API contract, missed sprint demo
Action: began documenting assumptions and proposing contracts after 24h
Outcome: next unclear spec was flagged same day and stub shipped
Quote: "I started writing down my assumptions in the ticket"
Follow-up: next unclear spec handled proactively
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Own it for junior level. The candidate described waiting on an API contract that caused a demo slip, then changed behavior by documenting assumptions and proposing contracts after 24 hours. The follow-up showed the new habit applied immediately on the next unclear task. This matches the expected scope for 0-2 years: individual work, clear learning from feedback, and local results. Biggest strength is the concrete, repeatable change rather than a one-off fix.

lowerTranscript.text: I was waiting on the design file for a button component and the project slipped a week because the designer was out. I didn't want to guess and get it wrong.
What did you do differently on the next task?
I just asked more questions in the next standup.

junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Own it for junior level. The candidate waited for a design file and accepted a week slip without attempting to unblock themselves. The follow-up change was limited to asking more questions in standup, which did not demonstrate initiative or learning beyond the immediate task. For 0-2 years the bar requires showing coachability and ownership of individual work; this example stays passive and externalizes the delay.

raiseTranscript.text: Two teams needed alignment on a shared data model before a quarterly launch. I waited for the architecture guild to publish the decision and the launch date slipped three weeks. After that I started running weekly syncs between the teams and wrote a lightweight decision log that anyone could update.
How did that affect later cross-team work?
The same two teams reused the log for three more decisions and cut alignment time by half.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you waited for instructions and it cost the work. What did you change after?
Role: senior owning cross-team data model
Situation: waited for guild decision, launch slipped three weeks
Action: created weekly syncs and shared decision log
Outcome: three later decisions reused the log and cut time by half
Quote: "I started running weekly syncs between the teams"
Follow-up: process reused by the same teams
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Own it for senior level. The candidate waited on an architecture guild decision that delayed a quarterly launch by three weeks, then introduced weekly syncs and a reusable decision log. The follow-up showed the change scaled to three additional decisions across teams. This meets the 3-7 year expectation of cross-team impact and influence without authority. Biggest strength is the measurable reuse of the new process rather than a single heroic effort.

lowerTranscript.text: We were blocked waiting for another team's API spec and the launch moved out a month. I escalated to my manager but nothing happened.
What process did you put in place afterward?
I made sure to check in with that team earlier in the next planning cycle.

senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Own it for senior level. The candidate accepted a month launch slip after waiting on an external API spec and relied solely on escalation. The follow-up change was limited to earlier check-ins, which did not create lasting cross-team leverage. At 3-7 years the bar requires evidence of influence without authority and repeatable mechanisms; this story shows neither.

raiseTranscript.text: We delayed a market expansion decision for six weeks waiting on a formal OKR from the CEO's staff. Revenue in that segment flattened while competitors moved. I then created a lightweight decision-rights framework that let regional leads move on 80 percent of opportunities without new exec sign-off.
What was the business result over the following year?
The framework was adopted by three regions and we closed the gap on two delayed opportunities within a quarter.

Follow-up: framework scaled across regions with measurable close rate
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Own it for exec level. The candidate waited on a formal OKR that delayed market expansion by six weeks and flattened revenue, then introduced a decision-rights framework that empowered regional leads on 80 percent of opportunities. The follow-up showed adoption by three regions and recovery of two delayed opportunities. This aligns with 10+ year expectations of org-level impact and strategic judgment under ambiguity. Biggest strength is the structural change that reduced future dependency rather than faster personal escalation.

I asked for clearer RACI on future big decisions.

At 10+ years the bar requires org-level mechanisms and judgment on ambiguity; this remained tactical and passive.
